captions.instagram:
How does Ayurveda work?

Half of India used an AYUSH system last year, and Ayurveda most of all. Build the five elements into vata, pitta and kapha, boil a kwatha down to a quarter, follow sarpagandha root into a blood-pressure pill, then run a fair trial and see how bias fools us.

→ Ayurveda's great texts, the Charaka and Sushruta Samhitas, grew in layers about 2,000 years ago.
→ Ayurveda says everything is made of five elements: space, air, fire, water and earth.
→ In the body they act as three doshas: vata moves, pitta transforms, kapha holds together.
→ A kwatha boils one part herb in 16 parts water down to a quarter: here 320 mL becomes 80 mL.
→ In 1949 a Mumbai cardiologist found sarpagandha root lowered blood pressure in most of his 50 patients.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/ayurvedaclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How does Ayurveda work? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
Half of India used an AYUSH system last year, and Ayurveda most of all. Build the five elements into vata, pitta and kapha, boil a kwatha down to a quarter, follow sarpagandha root into a blood-pressure pill, then run a fair trial and see how bias fools us.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/ayurvedaclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/ayurvedaclear

In this video:
• Three old books and a living system. Ayurveda, "knowledge of life", was written down in the Charaka and Sushruta Samhitas and Vagbhata's Ashtanga Hridaya, texts that grew in layers roughly 2,000 years ago.
• Five elements, three doshas. As Ayurveda describes it, space, air, fire, water and earth work in the body as three doshas: vata moves, pitta transforms, kapha holds together.
• Pulse, pot and routine. A vaidya asks, looks and may read the pulse with three fingers, a method first written down around the 13th century.
• From a snakeroot to a blood-pressure pill. In 1931 the Kolkata kaviraj Gananath Sen reported that sarpagandha root lowered blood pressure; in 1949 R.
• A fair test, and a safety check. Many people improve anyway, so fair trials randomise, blind and compare with a placebo.
• Using it wisely. Regular sleep, fresh plant-rich food, not overeating and daily exercise match modern advice.
